newsitem.title: USA: Last phase of Gingrich ethics probe is set.
newsitem.headline: Last phase of Gingrich ethics probe is set.

text.p: The House ethics committee said on Tuesday it will begin the final phase of its two-year investigation of charges against Speaker Newt Gingrich after he goes before the House for re-election.

The post of speaker is due to be filled at the start of the new Congress on Jan. 7. The ethics committee will meet the following day to begin a process it said would be completed no later than Jan. 21.

Gingrich has admitted charges by a four-member ethics panel that he violated House of Representatives rules by failing to ensure that a college course he taught complied with laws barring use of tax-exempt organisations for partisan political purposes and providing inaccurate information to investigators.
The 10-member ethics committee must decide what punishment to recommend to the full House.
Under the committee's schedule Republicans will not know what punishment is in store for the speaker when they are asked to vote for his re-election.
Gingrich's supporters have been calling for quick action by the committee so the issue would be settled before the election and have accused Democrats of foot-dragging.
The Republicans predicted the punishment would be a mild one that would not affect his speakership.

But some were said to be uneasy at the idea of voting while the issue is unresolved and one, Representative Michael Forbes of New York, a freshman supporter of Gingrich, called on Gingrich this week to step aside.
Gingrich's office has brushed aside Forbes' plea and is predicting the speaker will be re-elected without difficulty.
A meeting of House Republicans is set for next Monday and Gingrich is expected to face questions about the ethics affair from his colleagues.
The committee schedule was issued after telephone consultations between members, many of whom are scattered far from Washington.

It calls for a closed meeting on Jan. 8 to receive the findings of the investigative subcommittee and to vote on accepting Gingrich's waiver of a "trial" -- made unnecessary because he in effect pleaded guilty.

Following this meeting the committee will hold a public session to hear submissions by special counsel James Cole, who has spearheaded the investigation, and Gingrich's counsel on the question of punishment to be recommended to the full House.
It will then meet behind closed doors to consider the punishment.
The committee can recommend a variety of sanctions ranging all the way to expulsion, though no one thinks this would happen in the Gingrich case.
Other punishments include the serious one of censure, followed by a reprimand, a fine or denial of rights and privileges.
